newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu warns Israel-PLO peace in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu warns Israel-PLO peace in doubt.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has put the world on notice that Israel's historic peace process with the Palestinians begun in 1993 may be nearing the end of the road after a bloody marketplace bombing.

Netanyahu spoke out as Israel let pass a deadline in an ultimatum set out in a leaflet issued in the name of the Islamic Hamas group that claimed responsibility for last Wednesday's twin suicide bombings that killed 13 people and wounded 170.
It demanded Israel release all Palestinian prisoners. Israel said there were no plans to free anyone.

Thousands of police and troops remained on alert everywhere from bus stops to shopping malls despite the expiry of Sunday's 9 p.m. (1800 GMT) deadline. Police said they had "a series" of information warning of more attacks.

Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud bloc, told his cabinet on Sunday that Israel would not honour peace deals it signed with Yasser Arafat unless the Palestinian president cracked down on Islamic radicals.

"If Arafat honours his commitments in the agreement, chiefly to fight terrorism, the agreement will survive. If he doesn't, we will not keep up our part of the bargain unequivocally," an official statement quoted Netanyahu as saying.
He later told CBS-TV's "Face the Nation": "The whole peace is at stake. Arafat must make a choice and make it now."
Before winning elections in May 1996, Netanyahu opposed interim peace deals signed by the Labour party. In his campaign, however, he said he would honour signed accords.
Israeli opposition leader Ehud Barak blasted Netanyahu on Sunday over the prime minister's criticism of Arafat's alleged role in the resurgence of violence.

"Now they are trying to roll everything onto Arafat even before they know where the suicide attackers came from," Israel's Itim news agency quoted Barak, the Labour Party chief, as saying to kibbutz leaders in Tel Aviv.
Israeli and Palestinian officials have said they are not sure of the authenticity of the leaflet issued in Hamas's name.

Barak, a former army chief of staff who commanded Netanyahu in an elite unit, contended that the prime minister was "not responsible, not trustworthy, (does) not stand up to pressure". Barak likened Netanyahu's rule to that of "a blind goat".
He urged Netanyahu to "renew the trust between himself and the region's leadership".
Shortly before the ultimatum deadline passed, a Palestinian was shot dead in the West Bank in unclear circumstances.
Palestinians said a Jewish settler in a passing car shot the man. Police confirmed the man was found shot dead but said the shots fired from a car could have been an unrelated incident.
There have been fears Jewish militants might attack Palestinians in revenge for the Jerusalem bombings.
The double suicide bombing was the worst spasm of violence since Netanyahu took office and revived memories of a bombing spree in early 1996 in which Islamic militants killed 57 people.
Netanyahu won election in the wake of those bombings on a pledge to give Israelis peace with greater security.

The Israeli government suspended peace talks with the Palestinians in reaction to Wednesday's attack and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, preventing tens of thousands of Palestinians from reaching their jobs in the Jewish state.
It also threatened to enter Palestinian self-rule areas to fight militants if Arafat did not do the job.
Jibril Rajoub, the Palestinian Preventive Security chief in the West Bank, told Israel Television on Sunday that Palestinians would fight any Israeli entry into their areas.
"We would use all our means in order to defend ourselves, our honour, our sovereignty...I think it would drag us into an unprecedented situation," Rajoub said.
Top Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat, in an interview on Cable News Network, said Arafat had offered to join Netanyahu in fighting militants and had been spurned.
Israeli U.N. Ambassador-designate Dore Gold, with Erekat in the studio, said: "Well, I don't think that's exactly correct".
Gold did not elaborate but said that prior to the bombings, Palestinian officials linked cooperation in the fight against militants to "certain tangible (Israeli) concessions".

Palestinians have demanded Israel halt Jewish settlement of Arab lands taken in the 1967 Middle East War. They say the settlement policy pre-empts further peace talks, which ground to a virtual halt after Netanyahu broke ground for a new Jewish community in Arab East Jerusalem last March.
The new bombings prompted the postponement of U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross's mission to the region to jumpstart the peace talks. He is now expected towards the end of this week.

Arafat is to go to Jordan on Monday for talks with King Hussein on the deepening crisis, his office said. Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy's office said he would go to Egypt on Tuesday for discussions with President Hosni Mubarak.
